Introduction

pgBackRest provides backup and restore functions for PostgreSQL. It supports large databases and workloads.

pgBackRest v2.59.2 is the current stable release. Release notes are on the Releases page.

If you like pgBackRest, give the project a star on GitHub.

Features

Parallel Backup & Restore

Compression usually limits backup speed. pgBackRest uses parallel processing and efficient compression algorithms, such as lz4 and zstd, to reduce this limit.

Local or Remote Operation

A custom protocol lets pgBackRest back up, restore, and archive locally or remotely through TLS/SSH with minimal configuration. The protocol also provides an interface to query PostgreSQL. This interface removes the need for remote PostgreSQL access and improves security.

Multiple Repositories

You can use multiple repositories. For example, use a local repository with short retention for fast restores. Use a remote repository with longer retention for redundancy and access across the enterprise.

Full, Differential, & Incremental Backups (at File or Block Level)

pgBackRest supports full, differential, and incremental backups. It avoids the time resolution problems of rsync. Thus, differential and incremental backups are safe without a checksum calculation for each file. Block-level backups save space because they copy only the changed parts of files.

Backup Rotation & Archive Expiration

Set retention policies for full and differential backups to cover the required time frame. Keep the WAL archive for all backups or only the most recent backups. In the second case, the archive still keeps the WAL necessary to make older backups consistent.

Backup Integrity

pgBackRest calculates a checksum for every backup file. It checks each checksum again during a restore or verify operation. After it copies the backup files, it waits for all WAL segments necessary for backup consistency to reach the repository.

Repository backups can use the same format as a standard PostgreSQL cluster, including tablespaces. With compression disabled and hard links enabled, you can take a snapshot of a repository backup. You can then start a PostgreSQL cluster directly on the snapshot. This method helps with terabyte-scale databases, where a conventional restore takes a long time.

All operations use file and directory fsync to make changes durable.

Page Checksums

If page checksums are enabled, pgBackRest validates them for every file copied during a backup. A full backup validates all page checksums. Differential and incremental backups validate checksums in changed files.

Validation failures do not stop the backup. Console and file logs identify the pages that failed validation.

This feature detects page-level corruption before backups with valid copies of the data expire.

Backup Resume

You can resume an interrupted backup from its last position. pgBackRest compares checksums of previously copied files with the manifest to check their integrity. This operation can run entirely on the repository host, which reduces load on the PostgreSQL host. Checksum calculation also takes less time than compression and retransmission.

Streaming Compression & Checksums

pgBackRest calculates checksums and compresses data as it copies files to the repository. This applies to local and remote repositories.

For a repository on a separate host, pgBackRest compresses files on the PostgreSQL host. It transfers the compressed files and stores them on the repository host. When file compression is disabled, pgBackRest uses a lower compression level for transfers. This reduces bandwidth use with minimal CPU cost.

Delta Restore

The manifest contains a checksum for every backup file. A restore can use these checksums to substantially reduce processing time. A delta restore first removes files that are absent from the backup. It then calculates checksums for the remaining files. Files that match the backup stay in place; pgBackRest restores the other files as usual. Parallel processing can substantially reduce restore time.

Parallel, Asynchronous WAL Push & Get

Separate commands push WAL to the archive and get WAL from the archive. Both commands support parallel processing and asynchronous operation to reduce response time for PostgreSQL.

WAL push detects repeated WAL segments. It removes duplicates when the segments are identical and reports an error when they differ. Asynchronous WAL push transfers work to another process, which compresses segments in parallel for maximum throughput. This feature can be critical for databases with very high write volumes.

Asynchronous WAL get keeps a local queue of decompressed WAL segments ready for replay. This queue reduces the time to supply WAL to PostgreSQL and increases replay speed. Connections and storage with high latency, such as S3, benefit most.

The push and get commands compare PostgreSQL versions and system identifiers to check that the database and repository match. This check almost eliminates incorrect WAL archive locations.

Tablespace & Link Support

pgBackRest fully supports tablespaces. During a restore, you can map tablespaces to any location. You can also map all tablespaces to one location with one command. This is useful for development restores.

pgBackRest supports links for any file or directory in the PostgreSQL cluster. During a restore, you can restore all links to their original locations or map some or all links to new locations. You can also restore some or all links as regular files or directories inside the cluster directory.

S3, Azure, and GCS Compatible Object Store Support

pgBackRest repositories support S3, Azure, and GCS compatible object stores. These stores provide almost unlimited capacity and retention.

Encryption

pgBackRest can encrypt the repository to secure backups wherever they are stored.

Ransomware & Malware Protection

On versioned object storage, pgBackRest can read the repository at a specified point in time. Backups can be deleted or corrupted by an accident, malware, or ransomware. Set a target time before the damage to recover the data.

S3, Azure, and GCS compatible object stores support versioning. S3 object locking and GCS or Azure soft delete can provide more protection against tampering.

Compatibility with ten versions of PostgreSQL

pgBackRest supports ten PostgreSQL versions: the five supported versions and the last five EOL versions. This gives users time to upgrade to a supported version.

Contributions

pgBackRest welcomes contributions. See the Contributing Guidelines to contribute features, improvements, or issues.

Support

pgBackRest is completely free and open source under the MIT license. You may use it for personal or commercial purposes without any restrictions whatsoever. Bug reports are taken very seriously and will be addressed as quickly as possible. Please report bugs here.

A disaster recovery policy needs suitable replication and backup strategies. The design can be complex. You might need help with the architecture and ongoing support to keep your enterprise running.

Our sponsors offer products and services with pgBackRest support. They can help you meet your disaster recovery requirements.

pgBackRest 2.59.2 Released

September 27, 2026

The pgBackRest community released pgBackRest 2.59.2. This backup and restore solution supports PostgreSQL databases and workloads of all sizes.

pgBackRest provides these backup and recovery features: parallel backup and restore; full, differential, incremental, and block incremental backups; and multiple repositories. It also supports delta restore, parallel asynchronous archiving, malware/ransomware protection, per-file checksums, and validation of enabled page checksums during backup. Other features include multiple compression types, encryption, partial/failed backup resume, standby backups, tablespaces, and links. Storage options include S3, Azure, GCS, and SFTP. pgBackRest also supports backup expiration, local or remote operation through SSH or TLS, and flexible configuration.

Install pgBackRest from the PostgreSQL Yum Repository or PostgreSQL APT Repository. Many other distributions also provide packages. Download source code from releases.

New Features and Bug Fixes

  • PostgreSQL 19beta4 support (David Steele)
  • Fix empty block map when file is truncated to zero during backup (David Steele)
  • Disable read retry when filters are passed to the driver (David Steele)
  • Fix pagination of S3 version listing (David Steele)
  • Set the Azure version header for SAS authentication (David Steele)
  • Fix async archive-push stalling on a zero-size backup history file (Andrew Kroh)
  • Fix annotate command on a remote encrypted repository (Douglas J Hunley)

See the 2.59.2 Release Notes for additional fixes and improvements.

Important Notes

  • PostgreSQL 19beta4 changed pg_control and WAL formats. Clusters and WAL from earlier 19 beta versions are no longer supported. Recreate those clusters with 19beta4.

New Distribution Tarball

July 20, 2026

Starting with pgBackRest 2.59.0, each release includes a distribution tarball for simpler source builds. It contains generated source and prebuilt documentation. Unlike a Git checkout, it does not need code-generation or documentation tools to build and install pgBackRest.

The tarball contains source, pregenerated code, a command reference man page, HTML documentation, and a smoke test. Build it with meson and ninja and the usual pgBackRest libraries.

Each release includes pgbackrest-{version}.tar.gz and a matching .sha256sum checksum. Download them from GitHub releases. Follow the tarball README.md for build and test instructions.

Packagers should use the distribution tarball. This avoids the additional code-generation and documentation tools that future releases will require.

pgBackRest Will Continue!

May 18, 2026

pgBackRest will continue. During the previous few weeks, several sponsors agreed to fund ongoing development. The project no longer depends on one sponsor. This supports its long-term stability.

We thank each sponsor:

Amazon Web Services provides on-demand cloud resources for individuals, companies, and governments. It offers computing, storage, databases, machine learning, and more than 200 services with usage-based payment. It supports growth and invests in shared communities.

Supabase is a PostgreSQL backend platform. It lets developers build and scale applications without managing infrastructure. It includes a Postgres database, user authentication, real-time subscriptions, file storage, edge functions, and serverless functions. An active open-source community supports it.

pgEdge is an enterprise open-source Postgres platform for AI and high availability. It includes agentic AI tools, a DBA workbench, monitoring, incident response, flexible deployment, and maintenance without downtime. Deployments range from one node to active-active multi-master clusters in cloud, on-premises, or air-gapped environments.

Tiger Data created TimescaleDB, an open-source PostgreSQL time-series database. It also operates Tiger Cloud for managed time-series, analytics, and AI workloads. Self-managed and cloud options let organizations capture, store, and analyze time-series data at scale, from edge locations to centralized cloud deployments.

Percona provides open-source database software, support, and services to help organizations control their data infrastructure. It supports secure, efficient operation of MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Valkey, and Redis. Services include freely available software, 24/7 expert support, and practical database assistance.

Eon.io provides cloud infrastructure for backup, recovery, and data management. It helps teams store and access backups efficiently and use the data for analytics and AI. It offers fast, granular recovery and substantially lower storage costs for Postgres and data-intensive workloads across clouds. Recovery includes accidental data loss and AI agent regressions.

These organizations use pgBackRest for disaster recovery in their products and customer services. Their investment reflects its role in the PostgreSQL ecosystem. Their combined support sustains the project over the long term.

I look forward to resuming work on features and optimizations for upcoming releases. Thank you to our sponsors for funding this work. Thank you to the community for its patience and support during this transition.

Maintenance Update

May 4, 2026

After I announced that I would stop maintaining pgBackRest, I received many messages. Many expressed thanks and good wishes for my work over the years. It took time to read them.

Many users want pgBackRest to continue with me as primary maintainer, especially users who support others using pgBackRest. I also want this. However, after months of fundraising, I had concluded that it was not possible.

The situation has changed. I now expect to secure enough funding to continue the project. Several sponsors will fund pgBackRest, so one acquisition will no longer determine whether I can continue. We should also be able to add another maintainer to share the workload and provide continuity.

I understand the shock and uncertainty. Please give us time. The current pgBackRest version works, with no outstanding critical bugs or security issues. There is no immediate need to fork the project.

I expect to make a more definite announcement by the end of the week. Until then, we are actively working to resume pgBackRest development.

pgBackRest Is No Longer Being Maintained

April 27, 2026

pgBackRest is no longer maintained. If you fork it, choose a new project name.

After careful thought, I have decided to stop working on pgBackRest. I have worked on this project for thirteen years, with corporate sponsorship for much of that time. I also spent many nights and weekends developing it with numerous contributors. This reflects the substantial personal commitment that an open-source project can require.

Since the sale of Crunchy Data, I have maintained pgBackRest while seeking a position that would support this work. I have not found one. Sponsorship efforts have also raised much less than the project needs to remain viable.

I need to earn a living, and few roles involve pgBackRest. I can now consider other opportunities, but they will leave no time for this project. Maintenance, bug fixes, PR reviews, and issue responses already require substantial time. New features, the work I most enjoy, need additional time. I have therefore decided to stop completely instead of working irregularly or inadequately.

Someone might eventually fork pgBackRest. That would be a new project with new maintainers. They would need to earn trust, as we did.

Thank you to all pgBackRest contributors over the years. I enjoyed working with you.

2 - User Guide (Debian/Ubuntu)

Step-by-step pgBackRest setup and usage guide for Debian and Ubuntu systems.

Source: pgBackRest 2.59.2 user guide.

Introduction

Follow this guide in order the first time. Each section depends on earlier sections. For example, Restore requires the configuration from Quick Start. After pgBackRest is running, you can use sections independently.

These examples use Debian/Ubuntu and PostgreSQL 17. You can adapt them to other Unix distributions and PostgreSQL versions. Only commands to create, start, stop, and drop clusters depend on the OS. pgBackRest commands are the same across Unix systems, although the executable location can differ. PostgreSQL versions can differ in paths, file names, and settings; some examples show these differences.

Configuration information and documentation for PostgreSQL can be found in the PostgreSQL Manual.

The documentation build runs each command on a virtual machine from the XML source. This verifies that commands work in the specified order. Relevant output appears below each command. Other output is omitted to keep the instructions clear.

Run commands as an unprivileged user with sudo access to root and postgres. Alternatively, run each command directly as its specified user and remove sudo.

Concepts

The following definitions apply to pgBackRest, PostgreSQL, and this guide.

Backup

A backup is a consistent copy of a database cluster. Restore it to recover from hardware failure, perform Point-In-Time Recovery, or create a standby.

Full Backup: Copy all database cluster contents. The first cluster backup is always full. pgBackRest can restore it directly without files from another backup to achieve consistency.

Differential Backup: Copy files changed since the last full backup. Restore combines those files with unchanged files from that full backup. This uses less disk space than a full backup. Both the differential and its full backup must be valid for a restore.

Incremental Backup: Copy files changed since the last backup, whether full, differential, or incremental. Incremental backups are usually much smaller than full or differential backups. A restore requires valid versions of every backup in its dependency chain. This includes all incrementals back to the preceding differential, that differential, and its full backup. If no differential exists, it includes all incrementals back to the full backup and that full backup itself.

Restore

A restore copies backup files to a system where PostgreSQL can start them as a live cluster. It requires backup files and one or more WAL segments.

Write Ahead Log (WAL)

PostgreSQL uses WAL to prevent loss of committed changes. It writes transactions sequentially to WAL and considers them committed when those writes reach disk. A background process then writes the changes to the main database files, also called the heap. After a crash, WAL replay restores database consistency.

WAL is conceptually infinite but consists of individual 16MB segment files. A segment name has the form 0000000100000A1E000000FE. The first 8 hexadecimal digits identify the timeline. The next 16 identify the logical sequence number (LSN).

Encryption

Encryption converts data into a form that requires the correct password, also called a passphrase, to read.

pgBackRest encrypts the repository with a user-supplied password to prevent unauthorized access to its stored data.

Upgrading pgBackRest

Upgrading pgBackRest from v2.x to v2.y

To upgrade from v2.x to v2.y, most installations only need the new binaries. The repository format is unchanged. You can also downgrade unless you have used features that the older version does not support.

IMPORTANT:

Local and remote pgBackRest versions must match exactly. Upgrade them together. If versions differ, WAL archiving and backups fail until they match. The error is: [ProtocolError] expected value '2.x' for greeting key 'version' but got '2.y'.

Build

Prefer package installation to a source build. See Installation for package information.

Build from source on a separate build host. Production hosts generally should not have the required build tools. pgBackRest is one executable, which you can copy to other hosts after the build.

build ⇒ Download version 2.59.2 of pgBackRest to /build path

mkdir -p /build
curl -fsSL \
       https://github.com/pgbackrest/pgbackrest/releases/download/release%2F2.59.2/pgbackrest-2.59.2.tar.gz | \
       tar zx -C /build

build ⇒ Install build dependencies

sudo apt-get install python3-distutils meson gcc libpq-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev \
       pkg-config liblz4-dev libzstd-dev libbz2-dev libz-dev libssh2-1-dev libsystemd-dev

build ⇒ Configure and compile pgBackRest

meson setup /build/pgbackrest /build/pgbackrest-2.59.2
ninja -C /build/pgbackrest

build ⇒ Optionally run smoke tests to verify pgBackRest was built correctly

meson test -C /build/pgbackrest --suite smoke
ninja: Entering directory `/build/pgbackrest'
ninja: no work to do.
1/1 smoke OK               10.91s
       [filtered 7 lines of output]

Installation

Create a host named pg-primary for the demo cluster and pgBackRest examples.

Prefer package installation to a source build. Packages usually perform the remaining steps in this section. If a package omits a directory or sets incorrect permissions, create the directory or correct its permissions manually.

Debian/Ubuntu packages for pgBackRest are available at apt.postgresql.org.

If your distribution or version has no package, build from source and follow these manual installation steps.

pg-primary ⇒ Install dependencies

sudo apt-get install postgresql-client libxml2 libssh2-1

pg-primary ⇒ Copy pgBackRest binary from build host

sudo scp build:/build/pgbackrest/src/pgbackrest /usr/bin
sudo chmod 755 /usr/bin/pgbackrest

pgBackRest requires log and configuration directories and a configuration file.

pg-primary ⇒ Create pgBackRest configuration file and directories

sudo mkdir -p -m 770 /var/log/pgbackrest
sudo chown postgres:postgres /var/log/pgbackrest
sudo mkdir -p /etc/pgbackrest
sudo mkdir -p /etc/pgbackrest/conf.d
sudo touch /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf
sudo chmod 640 /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf
sudo chown postgres:postgres /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf

Check the installation. Running pgBackRest on the command line reports an error if a dependency is missing.

pg-primary ⇒ Make sure the installation worked

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest
pgBackRest 2.59.2 - General help

Usage:
    pgbackrest [options] [command]

Commands:
    annotate        add or modify backup annotation
    archive-get     get a WAL segment from the archive

    info            retrieve information about backups
    repo-get        get a file from a repository
    repo-ls         list files in a repository
    restore         restore a database cluster
    server          pgBackRest server
    server-ping     ping pgBackRest server
    stanza-create   create the required stanza data
    stanza-delete   delete a stanza
    stanza-upgrade  upgrade a stanza
    start           allow pgBackRest processes to run
    stop            stop pgBackRest processes from running
    verify          verify contents of a repository
    version         get version

Use 'pgbackrest help [command]' for more information.

Quick Start

Quick Start covers basic pgBackRest and PostgreSQL configuration. It introduces backup, restore, and info.

Setup Demo Cluster

The demo cluster is optional but strongly recommended, especially for new users. Examples use this cluster on the default port, 5432. Start it in a later section after configuration is complete.

pg-primary ⇒ Create the demo cluster

sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin/initdb \
       -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo -k -A peer

sudo pg_createcluster 17 demo
Configuring already existing cluster (configuration: /etc/postgresql/17/demo, data: /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo, owner: 102:103)
Ver Cluster Port Status Owner    Data directory              Log file
17  demo    5432 down   postgres /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-17-demo.log

Configure Cluster Stanza

A stanza contains the configuration for a PostgreSQL database cluster. It defines the cluster location, backup method, archive options, and other settings. Most database servers have one PostgreSQL cluster and one stanza. A backup server has a stanza for each cluster that needs a backup.

Choose a stanza name that describes the databases in the cluster. The primary and all replicas use the same stanza name. A functional name, such as app or dw, is preferable to a local cluster name, such as main or prod.

Use demo as the stanza name because it describes the cluster purpose.

pgBackRest needs the PostgreSQL base data directory. PostgreSQL can report it, but is unavailable during recovery. Set pg-path to exactly the data_directory value reported by PostgreSQL. Each backup compares these paths and fails if they differ.

Debian/Ubuntu stores clusters in /var/lib/postgresql/[version]/[cluster] by default. Use this location to identify the data directory.

When you create /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf, grant read access to the database owner, usually postgres.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure the PostgreSQL cluster data directory

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo

pgBackRest configuration files use a Windows INI-like format. Bracketed section names contain key/value pairs. Lines starting with # are comments; comments after a value on the same line are unsupported. Quoting is unsupported. pgBackRest trims whitespace from keys and values. Repeated sections are merged.

Configuration loading depends on these options:

  • Default config and config-include-path: load the default file if present. Append *.conf files from the default include path if present.
  • Explicit config: load only the specified file, which must exist.
  • Explicit config-include-path: load its *.conf files; the path must exist. Also load the default configuration file if present. Add --no-config to load only include-path files.
  • Explicit config and config-include-path: load the specified file and append *.conf files from the specified include path. The files must exist.
  • Explicit config-path: override the base path for the default configuration file and include path. Explicit config or config-include-path settings take precedence.

pgBackRest combines the files as one file, but each file must be valid independently. Each file must declare sections for its key/value pairs. File order does not determine precedence; sections do. The order from highest to lowest precedence is:

  • [stanza:command]
  • [stanza]
  • [global:command]
  • [global]

NOTE:

--config, --config-include-path and --config-path are command-line only options.

Environment variables can also configure pgBackRest, as shown below. They apply to commands such as backup, restore, and archive-push.

pg-primary ⇒ Configure log-path using the environment

sudo -u postgres bash -c ' \
       export PGBACKREST_LOG_PATH=/path/set/by/env && \
       pgbackrest --log-level-console=error help backup log-path'
pgBackRest 2.59.2 - 'backup' command - 'log-path' option help

Path where log files are stored.

The log path provides a location for pgBackRest to store log files. Note that
if log-level-file=off then no log path is required.
current: /path/set/by/env

default: /var/log/pgbackrest

Create the Repository

The repository is where pgBackRest stores backups and archives WAL segments.

To estimate repository space, take some backups. Record the sizes of full, incremental, and differential backups (full/incr/diff). Measure how much WAL the database generates each day. These measurements give an approximate space requirement. Requirements will probably change as the database changes.

This example stores the repository on the PostgreSQL host. This is the simplest configuration. It is useful when conventional backup software also backs up that host.

pg-primary ⇒ Create the pgBackRest repository

sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/pgbackrest
sudo chmod 750 /var/lib/pgbackrest
sudo chown postgres:postgres /var/lib/pgbackrest

Configure the repository path so pgBackRest can find it.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure the pgBackRest repository path

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest

You can configure multiple repositories. See Multiple Repositories.

Configure Archiving

Enable WAL archiving before backing up a running PostgreSQL cluster. PostgreSQL uses %p to specify the WAL segment location. A backup creates at least one WAL segment, even without explicit cluster writes.

pg-primary:/etc/postgresql/17/demo/postgresql.conf ⇒ Configure archive settings

archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=demo archive-push %p'
archive_mode = on

After these changes, restart the PostgreSQL cluster before taking a backup.

pg-primary ⇒ Restart the demo cluster

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo restart

Keep hot_standby enabled, which is the default, on every cluster. Any cluster might later become a standby, including a former primary after failover. A standby requires this setting to accept read-only connections.

If a WAL segment needs more than the default 60 seconds to reach the repository, increase pgBackRest archive-timeout. This differs from PostgreSQL archive_timeout, which forces a WAL segment switch during long inactive periods. See PostgreSQL Write Ahead Log for archive_timeout details.

Set command-specific options for archive-push. For example, a lower compression level can speed archiving without changing backup compression.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Config archive-push to use a lower compression level

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

Use command-specific configuration for any command. You can also limit it to one stanza, such as demo:archive-push.

Configure Retention

pgBackRest expires backups based on retention options.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure retention to 2 full backups

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=2
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

See Retention for more information.

Configure Repository Encryption

Set a repository cipher type and key to demonstrate encryption. Encryption always occurs on the client, even when storage such as S3 supports encryption.

Use a long, random passphrase for the cipher key. Generate one with openssl rand -base64 48.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure pgBackRest repository encryption

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=2
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

NOTE:

The example puts encryption settings in [global] so info can read all stanzas. Without stanza, info reads encryption settings only from [global]. For stanza-specific encryption, supply stanza to read the encrypted stanza.

After configuring the repository and creating and checking the stanza, you cannot change its encryption settings.

Create the Stanza

Run stanza-create to initialize the stanza. Then run check to verify archive and backup configuration.

pg-primary ⇒ Create the stanza and check the configuration

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --log-level-console=info stanza-create
P00   INFO: stanza-create command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=418-ea48493a --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --stanza=demo
P00   INFO: stanza-create for stanza 'demo' on repo1

P00   INFO: stanza-create command end: completed successfully

Check the Configuration

The check command validates pgBackRest and archive_command configuration for the specified stanza. It checks backup and archive settings for all repositories and databases configured on the current host. It detects configuration errors, especially archive errors that leave backups incomplete because required WAL segments never reached the archive. Run it on the PostgreSQL or repository host. You can also run it on a standby, but then it checks only repository configuration. A standby cannot execute pg_switch_xlog()/pg_switch_wal().

The command calls pg_create_restore_point('pgBackRest Archive Check') and pg_switch_xlog()/pg_switch_wal() to force PostgreSQL to archive a WAL segment.

pg-primary ⇒ Check the configuration

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --log-level-console=info check
P00   INFO: check command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=427-13fc86bf --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --stanza=demo
P00   INFO: check repo1 configuration (primary)
P00   INFO: check repo1 archive for WAL (primary)
P00   INFO: WAL segment 000000010000000000000001 successfully archived to '/var/lib/pgbackrest/archive/demo/17-1/0000000100000000/000000010000000000000001-d90c1b216d8173f5bcfd18f31ea16e25f9e9d786.gz' on repo1

P00   INFO: check command end: completed successfully

Performance Tuning

Some performance options are disabled by default to preserve repository compatibility. Enable the following options for new repositories. You can also enable them for existing repositories, but older pgBackRest versions might then be unable to read them. Compatibility depends on the feature introduction version shown below.

  • compress-type selects compression for backup and archive-push. The default is gz (Gzip). Prefer zst (Zstandard) for much faster processing with similar compression. Support started in v2.27. See Compress Type.
  • repo-bundle combines small files to save space and speed backup and restore, especially on object stores such as S3. It was introduced in v2.39. See File Bundling.
  • repo-block stores changed parts of files during diff/incr backup, which saves space and speeds backups. It was introduced in v2.46, but use at least v2.52.1. See Block Incremental.

Other performance options need additional configuration, or use safe defaults that are not optimal. These options are available in every v2 release.

  • process-max controls the number of processes. Its default, 1, is rarely suitable. Each command uses it differently; see the command documentation.
  • archive-async archives WAL in batches for much higher speed. It is disabled by default because it requires a spool path. See Asynchronous Archiving.
  • backup-standby reduces primary load by backing up from a standby. It is disabled by default because it needs extra configuration and at least one standby. See Backup from a Standby.

Perform a Backup

By default, backups wait for the next regular checkpoint. PostgreSQL checkpoint_timeout and checkpoint_segments settings can make this a long wait. Usually, set start-fast=y to force a checkpoint and start immediately. For a daily backup, one extra checkpoint should have little performance impact. On very busy clusters, use --start-fast on the command line only when needed.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure backup fast start

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=2
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

Run pgBackRest backup to back up the PostgreSQL cluster.

pg-primary ⇒ Backup the demo cluster

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo \
       --log-level-console=info backup
P00   INFO: backup command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=454-23b0197b --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo1-retention-full=2 --stanza=demo --start-fast

P00   WARN: no prior backup exists, incr backup has been changed to full

P00   INFO: execute backup start: backup begins after the requested immediate checkpoint completes
P00   INFO: backup start archive = 000000010000000000000002, lsn = 0/2000028
       [filtered 3 lines of output]
P00   INFO: check archive for segment(s) 000000010000000000000002:000000010000000000000003
P00   INFO: new backup label = 20260927-101911F

P00   INFO: full backup size = 22MB, file total = 963

P00   INFO: backup command end: completed successfully
P00   INFO: expire command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=454-23b0197b --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo1-retention-full=2 --stanza=demo

By default, pgBackRest attempts an incremental backup. An incremental requires a full backup. Because none existed, pgBackRest created a full backup.

Use type to select a full or differential backup.

pg-primary ⇒ Differential backup of the demo cluster

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=diff \
       --log-level-console=info backup
       [filtered 7 lines of output]
P00   INFO: check archive for segment(s) 000000010000000000000004:000000010000000000000005
P00   INFO: new backup label = 20260927-101911F_20260927-101914D

P00   INFO: diff backup size = 8.3KB, file total = 963

P00   INFO: backup command end: completed successfully
P00   INFO: expire command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=480-6911e174 --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo1-retention-full=2 --stanza=demo

No warning appeared because a full backup already existed. Incrementals can depend on a full or differential backup. Differentials must depend on a full backup. To create a full backup, run backup with --type=full.

During an online backup, pgBackRest waits for the archive to receive all WAL segments necessary for consistency. The archive-timeout default is 60 seconds. Increase it if an individual segment takes longer to archive.

Schedule a Backup

Backups can be scheduled with utilities such as cron.

The example schedules full backups at 6:30 AM each Sunday. It schedules differential backups at 6:30 AM Monday through Saturday. If installed midweek, the first differential job creates a full backup. The next day, it creates a differential.

#m h   dom mon dow   command
30 06  *   *   0     pgbackrest --type=full --stanza=demo backup
30 06  *   *   1-6   pgbackrest --type=diff --stanza=demo backup

After scheduling backups, configure regular expiration. See Retention.

Backup Information

Use the info command to get information about backups.

pg-primary ⇒ Get info for the demo cluster

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest info
stanza: demo
    status: ok
    cipher: aes-256-cbc

    db (current)
        wal archive min/max (17): 000000010000000000000001/000000010000000000000005
        full backup: 20260927-101911F
            timestamp start/stop: 2026-09-27 10:19:11+00 / 2026-09-27 10:19:14+00
            wal start/stop: 000000010000000000000002 / 000000010000000000000003
            database size: 22MB, database backup size: 22MB
            repo1: backup set size: 2.9MB, backup size: 2.9MB
        diff backup: 20260927-101911F_20260927-101914D
            timestamp start/stop: 2026-09-27 10:19:14+00 / 2026-09-27 10:19:16+00
            wal start/stop: 000000010000000000000004 / 000000010000000000000005
            database size: 22MB, database backup size: 8.3KB
            repo1: backup set size: 2.9MB, backup size: 464B
            backup reference total: 1 full

The info command reports on one stanza or all stanzas. By default, text output summarizes backups for the requested stanzas. The text format can change in any release.

For machine-readable output, use --output=json. JSON includes much more information than text output. Its format stays stable unless a bug requires a change.

Use --detail-level=progress to show only progress and reduce execution time. This skips all checks except stanza availability.

Each stanza has a separate section. Use --stanza to show only one. The status field indicates stanza health: ok means pgBackRest operates normally. With multiple repositories, mixed means at least one repository has an unhealthy stanza; output then gives the status per repository. An unknown repository error uses the code other and includes full error details.

The wal archive min/max field shows the minimum and maximum archived WAL. With multiple repositories, it covers all repositories unless you set --repo. Archive retention policies or other causes can leave gaps in this range.

The backup/expire running and/or restore running messages appear beside status when those commands run on the host. Text output also shows progress per repository. JSON output includes a repo array.

Backups appear from oldest to newest. The oldest is always a full backup, with an F at the end of its label. The newest can be full, differential (label ends with D), or incremental (label ends with I).

The timestamp start/stop field shows when the backup ran. Use timestamp stop to select a backup for Point-In-Time Recovery. See Point-In-Time Recovery.

The wal start/stop field shows the WAL range necessary for database consistency after a restore. The backup command checks that the archive contains this range before it completes.

The database size field shows the full, uncompressed database size. The database backup size field shows the database data actually backed up. These values match for full backups.

The repo field identifies the repository that contains the backup. The backup set size includes files in this backup and referenced backups needed for a restore. The backup size includes only files in this backup. These sizes match for full backups. When pgBackRest compression is enabled, repository sizes reflect compressed files.

The backup reference total summarizes other backups needed to restore this backup. Use --set for the complete reference list.

Restore a Backup

Backups protect against failures, including hardware failure and data corruption. For this example, simulate corruption by removing an essential cluster file.

pg-primary ⇒ Stop the demo cluster and delete the pg_control file

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo stop
sudo -u postgres rm /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/global/pg_control

Starting the cluster without this file produces an error.

pg-primary ⇒ Attempt to start the corrupted demo cluster

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo start
Error: /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin/pg_ctl /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin/pg_ctl start -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo -l /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-17-demo.log -s -o  -c config_file="/etc/postgresql/17/demo/postgresql.conf"  exited with status 1:

postgres: could not find the database system

Expected to find it in the directory "/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo",
but could not open file "/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/global/pg_control": No such file or directory
Examine the log output.

Run pgBackRest restore to restore the PostgreSQL cluster. First stop the cluster, which is already stopped in this example. Remove all files from its data directory.

pg-primary ⇒ Remove old files from demo cluster

sudo -u postgres find /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo -mindepth 1 -delete

pg-primary ⇒ Restore the demo cluster and start PostgreSQL

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo restore
sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo start

The cluster started because the restore replaced the missing pg_control file.

See Restore for more information about restore.

Monitoring

Monitor production systems. You can integrate pgBackRest with many monitoring tools.

pgBackRest JSON output includes all backups for each stanza and WAL archive information.

In PostgreSQL

Use PostgreSQL COPY to load pgBackRest information into a table. This example puts that logic in a function for real-time queries.

pg-primary ⇒ Load pgBackRest info function for PostgreSQL

sudo -u postgres cat \
       /var/lib/postgresql/pgbackrest/doc/example/pgsql-pgbackrest-info.sql
-- An example of monitoring pgBackRest from within PostgreSQL
--
-- Use copy to export data from the pgBackRest info command into the jsonb
-- type so it can be queried directly by PostgreSQL.

-- Create monitor schema
create schema monitor;

-- Get pgBackRest info in JSON format
create function monitor.pgbackrest_info()
    returns jsonb AS $$
declare
    data jsonb;
begin
    -- Create a temp table to hold the JSON data
    create temp table temp_pgbackrest_data (data text);

    -- Copy data into the table directly from the pgBackRest info command
    copy temp_pgbackrest_data (data)
        from program
            'pgbackrest --output=json info' (format text);

    select replace(temp_pgbackrest_data.data, E'\n', '\n')::jsonb
      into data
      from temp_pgbackrest_data;

    drop table temp_pgbackrest_data;

    return data;
end $$ language plpgsql;
sudo -u postgres psql -f \
       /var/lib/postgresql/pgbackrest/doc/example/pgsql-pgbackrest-info.sql

Use monitor.pgbackrest_info() to find a stanza’s last successful backup time and archived WAL.

pg-primary ⇒ Query last successful backup time and archived WAL

sudo -u postgres cat \
       /var/lib/postgresql/pgbackrest/doc/example/pgsql-pgbackrest-query.sql
-- Get last successful backup for each stanza
--
-- Requires the monitor.pgbackrest_info function.
with stanza as
(
    select data->'name' as name,
           data->'backup'->(
               jsonb_array_length(data->'backup') - 1) as last_backup,
           data->'archive'->(
               jsonb_array_length(data->'archive') - 1) as current_archive
      from jsonb_array_elements(monitor.pgbackrest_info()) as data
)
select name,
       to_timestamp(
           (last_backup->'timestamp'->>'stop')::numeric) as last_successful_backup,
       current_archive->>'max' as last_archived_wal
  from stanza;
sudo -u postgres psql -f \
       /var/lib/postgresql/pgbackrest/doc/example/pgsql-pgbackrest-query.sql
  name  | last_successful_backup |    last_archived_wal
--------+------------------------+--------------------------
 "demo" | 2026-09-27 10:19:16+00 | 000000010000000000000005
(1 row)

Using jq

The jq command-line utility extracts data from JSON.

pg-primary ⇒ Install jq utility

sudo apt-get install jq

Use jq to query a stanza’s last successful backup time.

pg-primary ⇒ Query last successful backup time

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --output=json --stanza=demo info | \
       jq '.[0] | .backup[-1] | .timestamp.stop'
1790504356

You can also query the last archived WAL.

pg-primary ⇒ Query last archived WAL

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --output=json --stanza=demo info | \
       jq '.[0] | .archive[-1] | .max'
"000000010000000000000005"

NOTE:

This syntax requires jq v1.5.

NOTE:

jq may round large numbers such as system identifiers. Test your queries carefully.

Backup

With multiple repositories, pgBackRest backs up to the highest priority repository, such as repo1. Use --repo to select another repository.

pgBackRest has no built-in scheduler. Use cron or another scheduler to run it.

See Perform a Backup for more details and examples.

File Bundling

File bundles reduce backup time and repository space. Benefits are greatest on object stores, such as S3, and filesystems with large blocks. Object stores have higher per-file creation costs. Very small files can cost as much to store as larger files.

Enable file bundles with repo-bundle.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure repo1-bundle

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=2
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

A full backup without bundles has more than 1000 files in its backup path. Bundles substantially reduce this count. Zero-length files then have only manifest entries. Without bundles, each zero-length file is stored separately.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform a full backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=full backup

pg-primary ⇒ Check file total

sudo -u postgres find /var/lib/pgbackrest/backup/demo/latest/ -type f | wc -l
5

Tune bundles with repo-bundle-size and repo-bundle-limit. The defaults should suit most cases.

Bundles usually improve efficiency, but make manual file retrieval harder. They might also be unsuitable for deduplicated storage because each full backup arranges files differently. Bundles cannot resume after interruption. Avoid a very high repo-bundle-limit.

Block Incremental

Block incremental backups store only file parts changed since the previous backup. This saves space compared with storing entire files.

Enable block incremental backups with repo-block. They work best when enabled for every backup type. File bundles must also be enabled.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure repo1-block

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-block=y
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=2
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

Backup Annotations

Attach informative key/value pairs to the backup. Repeat this option to attach multiple annotations.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform a full backup with annotations

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --annotation=source="demo backup" \
       --annotation=key=value --type=full backup

When --set specifies a backup, the info command includes its annotations in text output. JSON output always includes annotations.

pg-primary ⇒ Get info for the demo cluster

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --set=20260927-101930F info
stanza: demo
    status: ok
    cipher: aes-256-cbc

    db (current)
        wal archive min/max (17): 000000020000000000000007/000000020000000000000009

        full backup: 20260927-101930F
            timestamp start/stop: 2026-09-27 10:19:30+00 / 2026-09-27 10:19:31+00
            wal start/stop: 000000020000000000000008 / 000000020000000000000009
            lsn start/stop: 0/8000028 / 0/9000050
            database size: 22MB, database backup size: 22MB
            repo1: backup size: 2.9MB
            database list: postgres (5)

            annotation(s)

                key: value
                source: demo backup

Use annotate to add, change, or remove annotations after the backup command creates a backup.

pg-primary ⇒ Change backup annotations

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --set=20260927-101930F \
       --annotation=key= --annotation=new_key=new_value annotate
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --set=20260927-101930F info
stanza: demo
    status: ok
    cipher: aes-256-cbc

    db (current)
        wal archive min/max (17): 000000020000000000000007/000000020000000000000009

        full backup: 20260927-101930F
            timestamp start/stop: 2026-09-27 10:19:30+00 / 2026-09-27 10:19:31+00
            wal start/stop: 000000020000000000000008 / 000000020000000000000009
            lsn start/stop: 0/8000028 / 0/9000050
            database size: 22MB, database backup size: 22MB
            repo1: backup size: 2.9MB
            database list: postgres (5)

            annotation(s)

                new_key: new_value
                source: demo backup

Retention

Retain as many backups as practical to extend the Point-in-Time Recovery window. Account for limits such as disk space. Retention options remove backups when they are no longer needed.

pgBackRest rotates full backups according to a count or time period. Count-based retention keeps a specified number, regardless of creation times. Differential retention uses a count, but a differential always expires with its parent full backup. Incremental backups have no independent expiration policy. They expire with their parent full or differential backup. See Full Backup Retention and Differential Backup Retention for examples.

By default, pgBackRest keeps archived WAL for unexpired backups. You can change this per repository with retention-archive options, but this is not recommended. See Archive Retention.

The expire command runs automatically after each successful backup. You can also run it manually. A manual run applies each configured repository’s retention settings; --repo limits it to one repository. Use --set to expire a specific backup set. Without --repo, pgBackRest searches all repositories and expires sets that match. Every expire run also checks and applies archive retention.

Full Backup Retention

repo1-retention-full-type determines whether repo1-retention-full means a backup count or days of retention. New backups must complete before expiration. With repo1-retention-full-type=count and repo1-retention-full=2, three full backups exist before the oldest expires. With repo1-retention-full-type=time and repo1-retention-full=20, at least one full backup must be 20 days old before expiration.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure repo1-retention-full

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-block=y
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=2
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

repo1-retention-full=2, but only one full backup exists. The next full backup will not expire any full backups.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform a full backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=full \
       --log-level-console=detail backup
       [filtered 975 lines of output]
P00   INFO: repo1: remove expired backup 20260927-101928F
P00 DETAIL: repo1: 17-1 archive retention on backup 20260927-101930F, start = 000000020000000000000008

P00   INFO: repo1: 17-1 remove archive, start = 000000020000000000000007, stop = 000000020000000000000007

P00   INFO: expire command end: completed successfully

Archive data does expire because WAL segments exist from before the oldest backup. These cannot recover that backup. Recovery uses WAL generated after a backup.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform a full backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=full \
       --log-level-console=info backup
       [filtered 11 lines of output]
P00   INFO: repo1: expire full backup 20260927-101930F
P00   INFO: repo1: remove expired backup 20260927-101930F
P00   INFO: repo1: 17-1 remove archive, start = 000000020000000000000008, stop = 000000020000000000000009

P00   INFO: expire command end: completed successfully

Full backup 20260927-101911F expires. Archive retention now follows 20260927-101932F, the oldest remaining full backup.

Differential Backup Retention

Set repo1-retention-diff to the required differential backup count. Differentials depend only on the previous full backup. Keep a changing set covering the last day or longer for fast recent restores with less total space.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure repo1-retention-diff

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-block=y
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-diff=1
repo1-retention-full=2
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

With repo1-retention-diff=1, two differentials must complete before one expires. Add an incremental to demonstrate that it expires with its parent differential.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform differential and incremental backups

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=diff backup
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=incr backup

The next differential backup expires the previous differential and its incremental. One differential remains.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform a differential backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=diff \
       --log-level-console=info backup
       [filtered 10 lines of output]
P00   INFO: backup command end: completed successfully
P00   INFO: expire command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=957-5a78b9e0 --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo1-retention-diff=1 --repo1-retention-full=2 --stanza=demo
P00   INFO: repo1: expire diff backup set 20260927-101935F_20260927-101937D, 20260927-101935F_20260927-101938I
P00   INFO: repo1: remove expired backup 20260927-101935F_20260927-101938I
P00   INFO: repo1: remove expired backup 20260927-101935F_20260927-101937D
P00   INFO: expire command end: completed successfully

Archive Retention

By default, archive expiration follows full backup expiration through repo1-retention-full. You can expire archives more aggressively to save disk space. For differential archive retention, full backups also count as differentials.

Archive expiration never removes WAL needed for backup consistency. However, PITR needs a continuous WAL stream. Use care when expiring archives beyond normal backup expiration. To inspect proposed removals, run expire with command-line dry-run.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure repo1-retention-diff

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-block=y
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-diff=2
repo1-retention-full=2
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

pg-primary ⇒ Perform differential backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=diff \
       --log-level-console=info backup
       [filtered 6 lines of output]
P00   INFO: backup stop archive = 000000020000000000000017, lsn = 0/17000050
P00   INFO: check archive for segment(s) 000000020000000000000016:000000020000000000000017
P00   INFO: new backup label = 20260927-101935F_20260927-101941D

P00   INFO: diff backup size = 8.3KB, file total = 963
P00   INFO: backup command end: completed successfully
       [filtered 2 lines of output]

pg-primary ⇒ Expire archive

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --log-level-console=detail \
       --repo1-retention-archive-type=diff --repo1-retention-archive=1 expire
P00   INFO: expire command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=1039-a1b1a5e3 --log-level-console=detail --no-log-timestamp --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo1-retention-archive=1 --repo1-retention-archive-type=diff --repo1-retention-diff=2 --repo1-retention-full=2 --stanza=demo
P00 DETAIL: repo1: 17-1 archive retention on backup 20260927-101932F, start = 00000002000000000000000A, stop = 00000002000000000000000B
P00 DETAIL: repo1: 17-1 archive retention on backup 20260927-101935F, start = 00000002000000000000000C, stop = 00000002000000000000000D
P00 DETAIL: repo1: 17-1 archive retention on backup 20260927-101935F_20260927-101939D, start = 000000020000000000000012, stop = 000000020000000000000013
P00 DETAIL: repo1: 17-1 archive retention on backup 20260927-101935F_20260927-101941D, start = 000000020000000000000016

P00   INFO: repo1: 17-1 remove archive, start = 00000002000000000000000E, stop = 000000020000000000000011
P00   INFO: repo1: 17-1 remove archive, start = 000000020000000000000014, stop = 000000020000000000000015

P00   INFO: expire command end: completed successfully

WAL for 20260927-101935F_20260927-101939D must remain to make older backups consistent, although those backups can no longer support further PITR. Segments generated after 20260927-101935F_20260927-101939D and before 20260927-101935F_20260927-101941D are removed. Segments after the new backup 20260927-101935F_20260927-101941D remain available for PITR.

Full backups count as differentials for differential archive retention. With these settings, a new full backup retains only its own archive for PITR.

Restore

By default, restore selects the latest backup from the first repository with backups. See Quick Start - Restore a Backup. Repository order comes from pgbackrest.conf; for example, repo1 precedes repo2. Use --repo, such as --repo=1, to select a repository. Use --set to select a backup other than the latest.

For PITR with --type=time or --type=lsn, specify the target time or LSN with --target. Without --set, pgBackRest searches configured repositories in order for a backup containing that time or LSN. If none matches, --type=time uses the latest backup in the first repository with backups. For --type=lsn, it selects no backup. For other types, such as xid, use --set if the target precedes the latest backup. See Point-in-Time Recovery.

Backups exclude replication slots, as PostgreSQL recommends. See Backing Up The Data Directory.

The following sections introduce additional restore command features.

File Ownership

A typical restore runs as a non-root user. All restored files belong to the executing user and group. Existing files with other ownership cause an error if pgBackRest cannot change their ownership. Have a privileged user correct the ownership before retrying.

When restore runs as root, pgBackRest attempts to recreate manifest ownership. The manifest stores user/group names, so matching names must exist locally. If a name is absent, use the PostgreSQL data directory owner or group. If that identity also lacks a name, use root.

Delta Option

Restore a Backup in Quick Start required an empty cluster directory before restore. The delta option identifies files that can remain and files that need replacement. It also removes files absent from the manifest, including divergent changes. pgBackRest calculates a SHA-1 hash for each existing file. A file whose SHA-1 differs from the backup is restored.

Use process-max to speed this operation. PostgreSQL is stopped during restore, so you can use more processes than during an online backup.

pg-primary ⇒ Stop the demo cluster, perform delta restore

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo stop
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --delta \
       --log-level-console=detail restore
       [filtered 2 lines of output]
P00 DETAIL: check '/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo' exists
P00 DETAIL: remove 'global/pg_control' so cluster will not start if restore does not complete

P00   INFO: remove invalid files/links/paths from '/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo'

P00 DETAIL: remove invalid file '/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/backup_label.old'
P00 DETAIL: remove invalid file '/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/base/1/pg_internal.init'
       [filtered 133 lines of output]

pg-primary ⇒ Restart PostgreSQL

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo start

Restore Selected Databases

Restore selected databases to improve performance or use a destination with insufficient space for the entire cluster backup.

Create test1 and test2 to demonstrate selective restore.

pg-primary ⇒ Create two test databases

sudo -u postgres psql -c "create database test1;"
CREATE DATABASE
sudo -u postgres psql -c "create database test2;"
CREATE DATABASE

Add tables and data to each test database to verify recovery after selective restore.

pg-primary ⇒ Create a test table in each database

sudo -u postgres psql -c "create table test1_table (id int); \
       insert into test1_table (id) values (1);" test1
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
sudo -u postgres psql -c "create table test2_table (id int); \
       insert into test2_table (id) values (2);" test2
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1

Take a new backup that includes the new databases.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform a backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=incr backup

Selective restore can save space. Record test1 disk use now for comparison after the restore.

pg-primary ⇒ Show space used by test1 database

sudo -u postgres du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/base/32768
7.4M	/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/base/32768

To find available databases, run info with set to list the backup set contents.

pg-primary ⇒ Show database list for backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo \
       --set=20260927-101935F_20260927-101948I info
       [filtered 12 lines of output]
            repo1: backup size: 1.9MB
            backup reference list: 20260927-101935F, 20260927-101935F_20260927-101941D

            database list: postgres (5), test1 (32768), test2 (32769)

Stop the cluster and restore only the test2 database. Built-in databases (template0, template1, and postgres) are always restored.

WARNING:

Recovery can fail without --type=immediate. After consistency, PostgreSQL treats zeroed pages as errors, even with full-page writes. PostgreSQL ≥ 13 can use ignore_invalid_pages to ignore invalid pages. If you use this setting, check recovery logs for invalid pages in the selected databases.

pg-primary ⇒ Restore from last backup including only the test2 database

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo stop
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --delta \
       --db-include=test2 --type=immediate --target-action=promote restore

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo start

After recovery, test2 contains all previously created tables and data.

pg-primary ⇒ Demonstrate that the test2 database was recovered

sudo -u postgres psql -c "select * from test2_table;" test2
 id
----
  2
(1 row)

Although recovery succeeded, test1 is inaccessible. Its files were restored as sparse, zeroed files. PostgreSQL can replay WAL into them, but empty essential files leave the database invalid. This intentionally prevents use of a database that might contain only partial data from WAL replay.

pg-primary ⇒ Attempting to connect to the test1 database will produce an error

sudo -u postgres psql -c "select * from test1_table;" test1
psql: error: connection to server on socket "/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432" failed: FATAL:  relation mapping file "base/32768/pg_filenode.map" contains invalid data

Sparse, zeroed test1 files use space only for WAL written during recovery. Backup and recovery WAL volumes can be substantial. However, they are usually a small fraction of database size, especially for large databases that benefit most from selective restore.

The selective restore uses much less disk space for test1 than a complete restore would.

pg-primary ⇒ Show space used by test1 database after recovery

sudo -u postgres du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/base/32768
8.0K	/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/base/32768

Only drop database can now operate on invalid test1. pgBackRest does not drop it automatically because this requires completed recovery and an accessible cluster.

pg-primary ⇒ Drop the test1 database

sudo -u postgres psql -c "drop database test1;"
DROP DATABASE

After dropping invalid test1, only test2 and the built-in databases remain.

pg-primary ⇒ List remaining databases

sudo -u postgres psql -c "select oid, datname from pg_database order by oid;"
  oid  |  datname
-------+-----------
     1 | template1
     4 | template0
     5 | postgres

 32769 | test2

(4 rows)

Point-in-Time Recovery

Restore a Backup in Quick Start replayed WAL to the end of the stream. This is usually best after hardware failure. For data corruption caused by machines or people, Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) is often more suitable.

PITR replays WAL from a backup to a specified LSN, time, transaction ID, or recovery point. Time-based recovery is often the most useful choice. This example recovers an accidentally dropped table. Use the same method for accidentally deleted data.

pg-primary ⇒ Create a table with very important data

sudo -u postgres psql -c "begin; \
       create table important_table (message text); \
       insert into important_table values ('Important Data'); \
       commit; \
       select * from important_table;"
       [filtered 4 lines of output]
    message
----------------

 Important Data

(1 row)

Use PostgreSQL time and include the timezone offset. This reduces unintended timezone conversions and unexpected recovery results.

pg-primary ⇒ Get the time from PostgreSQL

sudo -u postgres psql -Atc "select current_timestamp"
2026-09-27 10:19:58.808792+00

After recording the time, drop the table. In a real incident, the exact drop time can be harder or impossible to find. Investigation should help you estimate it.

pg-primary ⇒ Drop the important table

sudo -u postgres psql -c "begin; \
       drop table important_table; \
       commit; \
       select * from important_table;"
BEGIN
DROP TABLE
COMMITERROR:  relation "important_table" does not exist

LINE 1: ...le important_table;     commit;     select * from important_...
                                                             ^

A backup taken after the target cannot recover to that target. To demonstrate this, take an incremental backup without important_table.

pg-primary ⇒ Perform an incremental backup

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --type=incr backup
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest info
       [filtered 38 lines of output]
            backup reference total: 1 full, 1 diff
        incr backup: 20260927-101935F_20260927-102000I
            timestamp start/stop: 2026-09-27 10:20:00+00 / 2026-09-27 10:20:01+00
            wal start/stop: 00000004000000000000001A / 00000004000000000000001A
       [filtered 2 lines of output]

This backup cannot recover the lost table. PostgreSQL replays WAL forward and cannot reverse it.

pg-primary ⇒ Attempt recovery from an incorrect backup

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo stop
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --delta \
       --set=20260927-101935F_20260927-102000I --target-timeline=current \
       --type=time "--target=2026-09-27 10:19:58.808792+00" --target-action=promote restore

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo start
       [filtered 13 lines of output]
LOG:  database system is ready to accept read-only connections
LOG:  redo done at 0/1A000120 system usage: CPU: user: 0.00 s, system: 0.00 s, elapsed: 0.03 s

FATAL:  recovery ended before configured recovery target was reached
LOG:  startup process (PID 1440) exited with exit code 1
LOG:  terminating any other active server processes
LOG:  database system is shut down

Let pgBackRest select a backup that completed before the target time and can recover to it.

NOTE:

pgBackRest cannot automatically select a backup when the restore type is xid or name.

pg-primary ⇒ Restore the demo cluster to 2026-08-17 04:51:24.23782+00

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --delta \
       --type=time "--target=2026-09-27 10:19:58.808792+00" \
       --target-action=promote restore

sudo -u postgres cat /var/lib/postgresql/17/demo/postgresql.auto.conf
       [filtered 9 lines of output]
# Recovery settings generated by pgBackRest restore on 2026-09-27 10:20:03
restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=demo archive-get %f "%p"'
recovery_target_time = '2026-09-27 10:19:58.808792+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'

pgBackRest wrote recovery settings to postgresql.auto.conf, so start PostgreSQL immediately. PostgreSQL uses %f for the required WAL segment and %p for its destination. After recovery, the table exists and accepts queries again.

pg-primary ⇒ Start PostgreSQL and check that the important table exists

sudo -u postgres psql -c "select * from important_table"

Delete a Stanza

The stanza-delete command removes repository data for a stanza.

WARNING:

Use this command with care. It permanently removes every backup and archive for the specified stanza from the pgBackRest repository.

To delete a stanza:

  • Shut down the PostgreSQL cluster associated with the stanza (or use –force to override).
  • Run the stop command on the host where the stanza-delete command will be run.
  • Run the stanza-delete command.

After the command succeeds, remove the stanza from all applicable pgBackRest configuration files and environment variables.

Delete a stanza from one repository at a time. For multiple repositories, repeat stanza-delete with --repo for each repository.

pg-primary ⇒ Stop PostgreSQL cluster to be removed

sudo pg_ctlcluster 17 demo stop

pg-primary ⇒ Stop pgBackRest for the stanza

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --log-level-console=info stop
P00   INFO: stop command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=1572-06fe3d27 --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --stanza=demo

P00   INFO: stop command end: completed successfully

pg-primary ⇒ Delete the stanza from one repository

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --repo=1 \
       --log-level-console=info stanza-delete
P00   INFO: stanza-delete command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=1580-c06f14e0 --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo --repo=1 --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --stanza=demo

P00   INFO: stanza-delete command end: completed successfully

Multiple Repositories

Configure multiple repositories as shown in S3 Support. For example, use a local repository for fast restores and a remote repository for redundancy.

Commands such as stanza-create and stanza-upgrade automatically use all repositories. Others, such as stanza-delete, require a repo selection.

For compatibility, repo is optional when only repo1 is configured. It is required when the only repository has another index, such as repo2. This prevents command failures if another repository is added later.

archive-push sends WAL to all configured repositories. If one is unreachable, it still sends WAL to the others. Enable archive-async=y for effective independent progress. Otherwise, the other repositories can advance only one segment beyond the unreachable repository. If WAL cannot reach any repository, PostgreSQL keeps it in pg_wal. This can fill the volume.

Schedule backups separately for each repository. This lets you vary backup types and retention. Specify a repository for restores as well. A repository with low latency or cost is usually preferable, even with longer recovery time. Test restores to determine which is most efficient.

Azure-Compatible Object Store Support

pgBackRest supports repositories in Azure-compatible object stores. Create the container first; pgBackRest does not create it. You can use the container root (/). Usually, prefer a subpath so object-store logs and other data can share the container without conflicts.

WARNING:

Do not enable “hierarchical namespace” as this will cause errors during expire.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure Azure

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-block=y
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-diff=2
repo1-retention-full=2
repo2-azure-account=pgbackrest
repo2-azure-container=demo-container
repo2-azure-key=YXpLZXk=
repo2-path=/demo-repo
repo2-retention-full=4
repo2-type=azure
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

For a shared access signature, set repo2-azure-key-type to sas. Set repo2-azure-key to the signature token.

Run commands as you would for a repository on a local disk.

pg-primary ⇒ Create the stanza

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --log-level-console=info stanza-create
P00   INFO: stanza-create command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=1661-eeb7ca7a --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo --repo2-azure-account=<redacted> --repo2-azure-container=demo-container --repo2-azure-key=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo2-path=/demo-repo --repo2-type=azure --stanza=demo
P00   INFO: stanza-create for stanza 'demo' on repo1
P00   INFO: stanza-create for stanza 'demo' on repo2

P00   INFO: stanza-create command end: completed successfully

Azure file creation is relatively slow. Enable file bundling to improve backup/restore performance.

pg-primary ⇒ Backup the demo cluster

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --repo=2 \
       --log-level-console=info backup
P00   INFO: backup command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=1670-de551bc3 --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo --repo=2 --repo2-azure-account=<redacted> --repo2-azure-container=demo-container --repo2-azure-key=<redacted> --repo1-block --repo1-bundle --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo2-path=/demo-repo --repo1-retention-diff=2 --repo1-retention-full=2 --repo2-retention-full=4 --repo2-type=azure --stanza=demo --start-fast

P00   WARN: no prior backup exists, incr backup has been changed to full

P00   INFO: execute backup start: backup begins after the requested immediate checkpoint completes
P00   INFO: backup start archive = 00000005000000000000001B, lsn = 0/1B000028
       [filtered 3 lines of output]
P00   INFO: check archive for segment(s) 00000005000000000000001B:00000005000000000000001B
P00   INFO: new backup label = 20260927-102014F

P00   INFO: full backup size = 29.2MB, file total = 1265

P00   INFO: backup command end: completed successfully
P00   INFO: expire command begin 2.59.2: --exec-id=1670-de551bc3 --log-level-console=info --no-log-timestamp --repo=2 --repo2-azure-account=<redacted> --repo2-azure-container=demo-container --repo2-azure-key=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-pass=<redacted> --repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc --repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest --repo2-path=/demo-repo --repo1-retention-diff=2 --repo1-retention-full=2 --repo2-retention-full=4 --repo2-type=azure --stanza=demo

S3-Compatible Object Store Support

pgBackRest supports repositories in S3-compatible object stores. Create the bucket first; pgBackRest does not create it. You can use the bucket root (/). Usually, prefer a subpath so object-store logs and other data can share the bucket without conflicts.

pg-primary:/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf ⇒ Configure S3

[demo]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/17/demo
[global]
repo1-block=y
repo1-bundle=y
repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB+cgFDFl7MxGlgkZSaoPvTGirhPygu4jOKOXf9LO4vjfO
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-path=/var/lib/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-diff=2
repo1-retention-full=2
repo2-azure-account=pgbackrest
repo2-azure-container=demo-container
repo2-azure-key=YXpLZXk=
repo2-path=/demo-repo
repo2-retention-full=4
repo2-type=azure
repo3-path=/demo-repo
repo3-retention-full=4
repo3-s3-bucket=demo-bucket
repo3-s3-endpoint=s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
repo3-s3-key=accessKey1
repo3-s3-key-secret=verySecretKey1
repo3-s3-region=us-east-1
repo3-type=s3
start-fast=y
[global:archive-push]
compress-level=3

NOTE:

Set the region and endpoint for the bucket location. These examples use us-east-1.

Create a role for pgBackRest and restrict bucket permissions as much as possible. For an AWS instance-associated role, set repo3-s3-key-type=auto to retrieve temporary credentials automatically. You then do not need explicit keys in /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf.

This sample Amazon S3 policy will restrict all reads and writes to the bucket and repository path.

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:ListBucket"
            ],
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:s3:::demo-bucket"
            ],
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "s3:prefix": [
                        "",
                        "demo-repo"
                    ],
                    "s3:delimiter": [
                        "/"
                    ]
                }
            }
        },
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:ListBucket"
            ],
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:s3:::demo-bucket"
            ],
            "Condition": {
                "StringLike": {
                    "s3:prefix": [
                        "demo-repo/*"
                    ]
                }
            }
        },
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:PutObject",
                "s3:PutObjectTagging",
                "s3:GetObject",
                "s3:GetObjectVersion",
                "s3:DeleteObject"
            ],
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:s3:::demo-bucket/demo-repo/*"
            ]
        }
    ]
}

Run commands as you would for a repository on a local disk.

pg-primary ⇒ Create the stanza

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=demo --log-level-console=info stanza-create
       [filtered 4 lines of output]
P00   INFO: stanza 'demo' already exists on repo2 and is valid
P00   INFO: stanza-create for stanza 'demo' on repo3

P00   INFO: stanza-create command end: completed successfully

S3 file creation is relatively slow. Enable file bundling to improve backup/restore performance.
